about.title: About OpenNavo
about.description: What OpenNavo is, where its data comes from, and how we treat your information.

security.metaTitle: Free Antivirus for Mac, Powered by ClamAV · OpenNavo
security.description: Free, open-source malware scanning for Mac with ClamAV. Checks installers before they install, new downloads, startup items and app signatures.

hero.title: Free, open-source antivirus for Mac,
hero.lede: OpenNavo scans your Mac with the **ClamAV** engine and its official database, then adds **pre-install scans**, download checks, startup item reviews and signature check-ups. Everything runs on your Mac: no uploads, no account.

layers.title: Six checks, each with its own job.
layers.body: The virus database recognizes known malicious files. Signature, notarization and startup item checks cover what a database can’t see.

scan.title: The usual hiding spots in minutes, or the whole Mac.
scan.body: The engine uses about 1.1 GB of memory while scanning and quits after 5 idle minutes. Threats can be quarantined, deleted or trusted, and anything in quarantine can be restored.

quick.title: Quick Scan
quick.body: Programs that startup items run, Downloads, Desktop, temporary folders and apps installed in the last 7 days

full.title: Full Scan
full.body: The whole Mac, except the system volume, iCloud files not downloaded, Time Machine and network volumes

custom.title: Custom Scan
custom.body: Choose folders or an external drive

schedule.title: Scheduled scans
schedule.body: A quick scan at the time you set. It runs only while OpenNavo is open, skips when on battery and never wakes your Mac

startup.title: Everything that starts on its own, in one list.
startup.body: Twenty kinds of startup items, grouped by app, with signature, notarization and owner shown. New items trigger an alert right away, and anything you disable or remove can be restored.

points.trust: Apple, known developers and unsigned programs are told apart, so suspicious items stand out
points.alerts: An alert the moment a new startup item, login item or background service appears
points.restore: Items are backed up before they’re disabled or removed, so you can always restore them

startup.categoriesTitle: The 20 kinds of startup items it checks

posture.body: A read-only check of 11 system settings that changes nothing. When something needs fixing, OpenNavo opens the right pane in System Settings.

paste.title: Paste protection
paste.body: When you press ⌘V to paste a suspicious “download and run” command into a terminal, OpenNavo pauses and asks first. The check runs locally, and nothing you paste is stored.

virusTotal.title: VirusTotal lookup
virusTotal.body: Look up a file’s SHA-256 on VirusTotal with your own API key. Only the hash is sent; the file never leaves your Mac.

privacy.title: Your files stay on your Mac.

local.title: Scanned locally
local.body: Scans run on your Mac, and results are stored only there.

database.title: Official database
database.body: The database comes straight from ClamAV’s official servers, not through OpenNavo.

hashes.title: No uploads
hashes.body: The optional VirusTotal lookup sends only a file’s SHA-256, and only if you turn it on.

need.a: macOS ships with Gatekeeper, notarization and XProtect, which stop many known threats. Cracked software, installers from unknown sites and commands pasted into Terminal are still common ways in. OpenNavo adds a check at each of those points. It complements the protection in macOS rather than replacing it.

database.q: Where does the virus database come from, and how often is it updated?
database.a: It’s ClamAV’s official database, downloaded straight from ClamAV’s servers rather than through OpenNavo. The first download is about 113 MB (about 170 MB on disk). After that, OpenNavo checks every 4 hours by default and downloads only the changes.

performance.q: Will it slow my Mac down?
performance.a: The engine uses about 1.1 GB of memory while scanning and quits after 5 idle minutes, so it uses nothing the rest of the time. Scheduled scans run only while OpenNavo is open, skip when on battery and never wake your Mac.

upload.a: No. Scans run on your Mac and results stay there. The optional VirusTotal lookup has to be turned on with your own API key, and even then it sends only the file’s SHA-256.

realtime.q: Does it block malware in real time?
realtime.a: New downloads and new startup items are checked as soon as they appear, and you’re alerted right away, but OpenNavo can’t yet stop a program before its first run. Real-time blocking needs Apple’s Endpoint Security entitlement and will come once it’s granted.

coverage.q: Will it catch every piece of Mac malware?
coverage.a: No antivirus can promise that. ClamAV’s coverage of Mac-specific malware is limited, which is why OpenNavo also checks signatures, notarization and startup items, and shows the status of XProtect. Ordinary files over 100 MB, and installers over 1 GB or over 2 GB once unpacked, aren’t fully scanned.

price.a: Yes, and it needs no account. OpenNavo is open source under GPL-3.0, with its code on GitHub.

cta.title: Give your Mac one more check.
cta.body: OpenNavo is free, open source and runs on macOS 13 or later. The first time you scan, it asks before downloading the official database.

identity.intro: The same label can come from different programs. On your Mac, all of these should match before you treat it as part of an app that declares it:

where.title: Where it usually lives
where.launchd: A launch agent or daemon is usually defined by a property list named after its label ({file}) in one of these folders:
where.loginItem: Login items are listed in System Settings → General → Login Items & Extensions (Login Items on macOS 13 and 14).
where.receipt: macOS’s installer keeps package receipts: a record of the files an installer package put on your Mac. You can read one in Terminal with {command}.
where.malware: These folders are also where Mac malware most often sets itself up to start automatically, so an item there you don’t recognize is worth a check.

turnOff.title: How to turn it off in System Settings
turnOff.open: Open System Settings → General → Login Items & Extensions (Login Items on macOS 13 and 14).
turnOff.find: Under Allow in the Background, find the app or its developer.
turnOff.switch: Turn off its switch. Items that run for all users may ask for an administrator password.
turnOff.openAtLogin: Apps listed under Open at Login can be removed there: select one and click the minus button.
turnOff.note: Turning it off only stops it from starting automatically; it doesn’t delete any files. Uninstalling the app removes them. If you still use the app, its updates, syncing or other background features may stop working.

openNavo.title: Manage it with OpenNavo
openNavo.body: If this item is on your Mac, OpenNavo’s Startup Items lists it with its signature, its file location and the app OpenNavo matches it to on your Mac. You can turn it off or remove it there, and restore a removed item later.
openNavo.hint: Opens a preview only: OpenNavo looks for this label on your Mac and shows what it finds. Nothing is turned off or deleted until you confirm. Requires OpenNavo for Mac.

apps.title: Other Mac security apps in the catalog

backgroundItems.title: Background items
backgroundItems.body: What login items and launch agents are, which apps declare them, and how to turn them off.

firewall.metaTitle: Free Mac App Firewall for Outgoing Connections · OpenNavo
firewall.description: OpenNavo’s app firewall asks before each Mac app connects to the internet, then allows or blocks it by your rules. Free and open source, adapted from LuLu, and decided on your Mac.

hero.title: A firewall that asks before your apps connect.
hero.lede: The firewall built into macOS only screens **incoming** connections. OpenNavo’s app firewall watches the other direction: the first time an app connects to the network, it asks whether to allow or block it, and remembers your answer. Free and open source.

what.title: What it does
what.body: Every rule is yours, and everything is decided on this Mac.

ask.title: Asks before apps connect
ask.body: See which app it is, where it’s connecting and who signed it, then allow or block it.

rules.title: Rules by app, site or port
rules.body: Allow a whole app, or allow or block just one domain, IP range or port. More specific rules win, and at the same level Block wins over Allow.

blocklists.title: Block lists
blocklists.body: Import hosts files or lists of ad, tracking or malicious sites. Matching connections are blocked without asking, and lists from a web address update daily.

modes.title: Fewer questions when you want
modes.body: Connections without a rule can ask you, be allowed and logged, or be blocked and logged. Apple programs and apps you already have can be allowed automatically.

how.title: How it works on your Mac
how.body: The app firewall is a network system extension. The first time you turn it on, macOS asks you twice: allow OpenNavo’s system extension in System Settings, then allow it to filter network content. Connection details stay on your Mac and are never uploaded.
how.note: It needs macOS 13 or later and the release version of OpenNavo in the Applications folder.

items.incoming: It only covers connections that apps on this Mac start. Incoming connections are the job of the firewall built into macOS (System Settings → Network → Firewall).
items.notRunning: While OpenNavo isn’t running it can’t ask, so a connection without a rule is allowed for now and logged under Activity. Your existing rules keep applying.
items.directIp: Some apps look up an address themselves and connect straight to an IP, so blocking a domain can miss them; only IPs on a list stop those connections.
items.release: The app firewall ships only in the signed release version. Development and unsigned builds don’t include it.

origin.title: Adapted from LuLu
origin.body: The app firewall’s network filter adapts LuLu 4.5.1, the free, open-source firewall by Objective-See (Patrick Wardle), under the GPL-3.0 license. OpenNavo rewrote its rule handling, storage and interface, and isn’t affiliated with or endorsed by Objective-See. OpenNavo’s own code is open source under GPL-3.0 as well, and public on GitHub.

builtIn.q: Doesn’t a Mac already have a firewall?
builtIn.a: It does. macOS includes a firewall in System Settings → Network → Firewall. It controls incoming connections, which matters most on public Wi-Fi. It doesn’t ask you when an app connects out to the internet; an app firewall covers that part.

free.a: Yes, and there’s no account. OpenNavo, including the app firewall, is open source under the GPL-3.0 license.

breakApps.q: Will it stop my apps from working?
breakApps.a: Apps you block can’t connect, which can stop their updates or syncing. If you’d rather not be asked so often, set connections without a rule to Allow & Log and review them under Activity, or allow the apps you already have automatically.

privacy.q: Does it send my connections anywhere?
privacy.a: No. Rules and decisions are made on your Mac, and connection details aren’t uploaded. Block lists you add from a web address are downloaded to your Mac and checked there.

remove.a: In OpenNavo, open App Firewall → Settings and choose Remove. That turns off filtering and uninstalls the system extension, deleting your rules and activity log. macOS may ask for your password.

cta.title: Turn on the app firewall.
cta.body: OpenNavo is free and open source for macOS 13 and later. After installing it, open App Firewall and confirm the two macOS prompts.

clamav.metaTitle: ClamAV for Mac: Free Virus Scan and Its Limits · OpenNavo
clamav.description: Scan your Mac with the open-source ClamAV engine and its official virus database, for free. What ClamAV finds on a Mac, what it misses, and the extra checks OpenNavo adds.

hero.title: ClamAV on your Mac, without the Terminal.
hero.lede: **ClamAV** is a widely used open-source antivirus engine. OpenNavo runs it with the official virus database and adds quick, full and scheduled scans, plus a check before you install. It’s free, and your files never leave your Mac.

what.title: What ClamAV is
what.body: ClamAV is an open-source antivirus engine maintained by Cisco Talos and released under GPL-2.0. It recognizes known malicious files by matching them against its signature database, which keeps being updated. On its own it’s a set of command-line tools: after installing it with Homebrew (**brew install clamav**), freshclam downloads the database and clamscan scans files.

database.title: The official database
database.body: Downloaded straight from ClamAV’s official servers, not through OpenNavo: about 113 MB the first time, then only what changed. Updates are checked every 4 hours by default.

scans.title: Quick, full, custom and scheduled scans
scans.body: A quick scan covers what startup items run, Downloads, the Desktop, temporary folders and apps installed in the last 7 days. A full scan covers the whole Mac except the system volume, iCloud files that aren’t downloaded, Time Machine and network volumes.

install.title: Scans before installing
install.body: Apps installed through OpenNavo are scanned after Homebrew downloads them and before they’re installed. If a threat is found, the install stops.

quarantine.title: A quarantine you can undo
quarantine.body: Threats go to quarantine by default, so you can restore a file if it turns out to be a false alarm.

resources.title: Memory only while scanning
resources.body: The engine uses about 1.1 GB of memory while scanning and quits after 5 idle minutes.

limits.title: Where ClamAV falls short on a Mac

items.coverage: Its database covers Mac-specific malware only partly, so a scan that finds nothing doesn’t prove a Mac is clean.
items.signatures: It recognizes known threats by their signatures. New or changed malware can go unnoticed until signatures for it are added.
items.realtime: OpenNavo can’t stop a program before its first run yet: that needs Apple’s Endpoint Security entitlement. New downloads and new startup items are checked as soon as they appear.
items.large: Ordinary files over 100 MB, and installers over 1 GB or over 2 GB unpacked, aren’t scanned in full.

extras.title: What OpenNavo checks besides ClamAV
extras.body: These checks cover what a virus database can’t see:

signatures.title: Signatures and notarization
signatures.body: Installed apps’ signatures and notarization are checked, with an alert if an app’s developer signature changes.

startup.title: Startup items
startup.body: 20 kinds of startup items, from launch agents to browser extensions, with who signed each one and which app it belongs to.

posture.title: System check-up
posture.body: 11 macOS settings, including Gatekeeper, FileVault and the state of Apple’s XProtect, so you see at a glance what’s off.

virusTotal.title: Optional VirusTotal lookup
virusTotal.body: With your own API key, look up a file’s SHA-256 on VirusTotal. Only the hash is sent; files are never uploaded.

xprotect.q: Is ClamAV the same as XProtect?
xprotect.a: No. XProtect is the malware protection Apple builds into macOS, with Apple’s own rules. ClamAV is a separate open-source engine with its own database. OpenNavo scans with ClamAV and also shows whether XProtect is up to date.

free.a: Yes. ClamAV is open source, its database is free, and OpenNavo is open source under GPL-3.0, with no account needed.

upload.a: No. Scans run on your Mac and the results stay there. The optional VirusTotal lookup only sends a file’s SHA-256, and only after you turn it on.

terminal.q: Can I use ClamAV without OpenNavo?
terminal.a: Yes. Install it with Homebrew (brew install clamav), set up freshclam to download the database, then scan with clamscan. OpenNavo does the same in a window, with scheduled scans and a quarantine.

cta.title: Scan your Mac with ClamAV.
cta.body: OpenNavo is free and open source for macOS 13 and later. The first time you scan, it asks before downloading the official virus database.

xprotect.metaTitle: What Is XProtect on Mac? Built-in Malware Protection and Its Limits · OpenNavo
xprotect.description: XProtect is the malware protection Apple builds into macOS. How it works, what it misses, how to check it’s up to date, and what OpenNavo adds.

hero.title: XProtect: the antivirus already on your Mac.
hero.lede: Every Mac comes with **XProtect**, Apple’s built-in protection against known malware. It works quietly in the background, which also means you rarely see what it checks. Here’s what it does, where it stops, and how to make sure it’s up to date.

signatures.title: Recognizes known malware
signatures.body: XProtect uses signature rules (YARA) that Apple writes for malware it has found, and updates them on its own schedule, separately from macOS updates.

checks.title: Checks apps when they run
checks.body: It checks an app when it’s first opened, when it has changed and when its rules are updated. If it finds known malware, macOS blocks it and offers to move it to the Trash.

remediation.title: Removes some infections
remediation.body: Recent versions of macOS also look for malware XProtect knows about in the background, and remove it.

gatekeeper.title: Works with Gatekeeper and notarization
gatekeeper.body: Gatekeeper and notarization check who signed an app and that Apple scanned it; XProtect looks for malware Apple already knows.

items.known: It only knows what Apple knows. New malware, or a variant changed enough to slip past the rules, can run until Apple adds signatures for it.
items.updates: Its updates depend on a setting. XProtect’s rules arrive as security responses and system files, so if Install Security Responses and system files is off in Software Update’s automatic updates, they can fall behind.
items.visibility: You don’t see it work: there’s no XProtect window, no scan button and no report of what it checked.

check.title: How to check that XProtect is up to date

steps.systemInformation: Hold down Option, choose Apple menu → System Information, then open Software → Installations and look for recent entries whose names start with XProtect.
steps.terminal: Or run system_profiler SPInstallHistoryDataType in Terminal and look for the XProtect entries in its output.
steps.settings: In System Settings → General → Software Update, click the info button next to Automatic Updates and make sure Install Security Responses and system files is on.

check.note: OpenNavo’s system check-up reads XProtect’s version and when it was last updated, warns you if it hasn’t been updated for over 30 days, and checks that security responses install automatically.

extras.title: What OpenNavo adds
extras.body: OpenNavo doesn’t replace XProtect. It adds the checks XProtect doesn’t tell you about:

scan.title: Virus scans with ClamAV
scan.body: Quick, full and scheduled scans with the open-source ClamAV engine, and a scan before anything you install through OpenNavo.

startup.title: Startup items
startup.body: Everything that starts by itself, with its signature and app, and an alert when something new appears.

signatures.title: Signature check-up
signatures.body: Installed apps’ signatures and notarization, with an alert if a developer signature changes.

enough.a: XProtect blocks malware Apple has signatures for and updates itself, so keep it on and up to date. It can’t catch what Apple hasn’t added yet, though, and it doesn’t show you what it checked. A second scanner and a look at your startup items add the checks it doesn’t make.

off.a: There’s no setting for it in System Settings. It’s part of macOS and protected along with the rest of the system.

where.q: Where is XProtect on my Mac?
where.a: Its rules live in /Library/Apple/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.bundle, which macOS protects from changes. You don’t need to open it: the update history above shows when it last changed.

clamav.q: How is XProtect different from ClamAV?
clamav.a: Both match files against signatures of known malware, but they’re separate. XProtect uses Apple’s own rules and runs automatically; ClamAV is an open-source engine with its own database that runs when you scan. OpenNavo scans with ClamAV and shows XProtect’s status.

cta.title: See what XProtect doesn’t show you.
cta.body: OpenNavo’s free system check-up shows whether XProtect is up to date, next to 10 other macOS security settings.

about.title: What is OpenNavo?
about.definition: OpenNavo is a free, open-source Homebrew GUI for Mac: it installs and updates Homebrew apps on your Mac in one click, and its website is a directory of Mac apps with release notes, system requirements and uninstall steps.

compare.caption: How OpenNavo differs from the Homebrew command line and the Mac App Store

opennavo.use: A website directory, plus a Mac app with a graphical interface.
opennavo.source: Homebrew apps download from the source each cask declares.
opennavo.scope: Casks, through the Homebrew on your Mac, and App Store apps once you sign in with your Apple Account. Other apps link to the developer’s official download.

homebrew.source: Homebrew’s package definitions, plus any third-party taps you add.
homebrew.scope: Formulae (command-line tools) and casks (apps), with brew install and brew upgrade.

appStore.use: The App Store app on your Mac.
appStore.scope: Apps you get through your Apple Account. Apps from other sources are updated by their developers.

links.appleInstall: Apple Support: install and uninstall App Store purchases
links.appleDownload: Apple Support: download apps on your Mac
links.appleUpdate: Apple Support: update apps with the App Store

window.label: The OpenNavo Mac app installing an app from Discover

security.title: Scanned before it installs. Watched after.
security.body: OpenNavo ships the open-source **ClamAV** engine, with its database updated straight from ClamAV’s official servers. Apps you install through OpenNavo are scanned before they install, and new downloads and new startup items are checked as soon as they appear. Scans run on your Mac, and **no files are uploaded**.

scan.title: Quick, full and scheduled scans
scan.body: A quick scan checks Downloads, the Desktop and startup items in minutes and can run every day or week. A full scan covers the whole Mac.

install.title: Scanned before install
install.body: After Homebrew downloads an app and before it installs, the download is scanned. A threat stops the install.

downloads.title: New downloads, checked
downloads.body: OpenNavo watches your Downloads folder and scans each file when it finishes. Installers also get a signature and notarization check.

startup.title: Startup items
startup.body: Twenty kinds, from background services and login items to browser extensions, each with its signature and owning app. New ones trigger an alert right away.

signatures.title: Signature check-up
signatures.body: Checks the signature and notarization of every installed app, and warns you when an app’s developer signature suddenly changes, a sign it may have been replaced.

posture.title: System check-up
posture.body: SIP, Gatekeeper, FileVault, the firewall, XProtect and six more settings, so you can see at a glance what’s switched off.

security.note: ClamAV’s coverage of Mac-specific malware is limited, so OpenNavo also checks signatures, notarization and startup items. It adds to the protection built into macOS; it doesn’t replace it.

demo.label: The OpenNavo Mac app finding a threat during a scan and moving it to quarantine
demo.caption: Animated demo: the file names and the detected threat are made up.
demo.title: Security
demo.subtitle: Check-up, virus scans, startup items and protection. Results stay on this Mac

quick.title: Quick Scan
quick.body: Programs that startup items run, Downloads, Desktop, temporary folders and apps installed in the last 7 days

full.title: Full Scan
full.body: The whole Mac, except the system volume, iCloud files not downloaded, Time Machine and network volumes

custom.title: Custom Scan
custom.body: Choose folders or an external drive

catalog.title: {count} Mac app in one place, installed in one click. | {count} Mac apps in one place, installed in one click.
catalog.body: Install, update and uninstall, all in one place. Rankings follow **real installs from the last 30 days**, and **editor’s picks** and **collections** help you find the good ones.

homebrew.title: The Homebrew catalog
homebrew.body: Synced daily from Homebrew’s official catalog. Homebrew does the installing and updating, and you can see every command and log line.

appStore.title: Mac App Store apps
appStore.body: Search App Store apps right in the app, with details straight from Apple. Sign in with your Apple Account to install and update them.

link.title: Developer downloads
link.body: Apps that aren’t in Homebrew link to the developer’s official download. OpenNavo doesn’t host installers, and it checks the signature once a download finishes.

details.title: Every version, on the record.
details.body: When Homebrew picks up a new version, it shows up here with the exact commit time. The **release notes** we write are translated into your language automatically, with the original one click away.

points.about: Descriptions, screenshots, and install details before you install
points.deps: Dependencies, conflicts, and install locations at a glance
points.languages: Ten languages, falling back to English or the original when a translation is missing

install.title: One click, installed.
install.body: Click Get on an app page and OpenNavo runs Homebrew on your Mac to install it. You can see **the exact command** and **every line of the log**. When administrator rights are needed, macOS asks for your password, and OpenNavo never stores it.

points.queue: Tasks run in a queue, can be canceled, and can be retried if they fail
points.scan: Downloads are scanned for malware before they install; a threat stops the install
points.history: Every install, update, and removal is recorded on your Mac

updates.title: Updates, handled.
updates.body: A daily check gathers updates from Homebrew, the App Store, Sparkle, Electron and GitHub, with the count in the **menu bar**. One click on **Update All** takes care of the rest.

points.schedule: Daily checks at a set time, with optional notifications
points.verify: Updates from outside Homebrew must carry the same developer signature, or they aren’t installed
points.rollback: Apps that support it roll back to the previous version in one click
points.pin: Pin an app or skip a version, and Update All leaves it alone

toolkit.title: It looks after your Mac, too.
toolkit.body: Uninstall apps along with their leftovers, see what a cleanup will free before it runs, and keep CPU, memory, temperatures and fans in your menu bar.

uninstall.title: Uninstall without leftovers
uninstall.body: Uninstall apps from Homebrew, the App Store or a developer’s site. Their data, caches, preferences and background items are found too, and files shared with other apps stay by default.

cleanup.title: Look first, then clean
cleanup.body: A read-only scan takes about 30 seconds and sorts what it finds into three risk tiers. Caches are deleted; leftovers go to the Trash, where you can undo. Keychains, VPNs and virtual machines are always protected.

monitor.title: Monitoring in the menu bar
monitor.body: CPU, GPU, memory, disk, network, battery, temperatures and fans: put any of them in the menu bar, and set fan speeds too.

handoff.title: Find on the web, install in the app
handoff.body: Click Open in OpenNavo on the web. The app shows the command it will run and installs only after you confirm.
handoff.dialogBody: This request came from a web page. OpenNavo will run:

mirrors.title: Mirror speed test
mirrors.body: OpenNavo tests the official source and the mirrors, then recommends the fastest. Homebrew setup and brew commands use it, and you can switch at any time.

brewfile.title: New Mac, same apps
brewfile.body: Add your apps to a list and export a Brewfile. On a new Mac, one command installs them all.

search.title: Search with ⌘K
search.body: Search by English name, Chinese name, pinyin, or common aliases. Typing vscode finds Visual Studio Code.

languages.title: Ten languages
languages.body: The interface speaks English, Simplified and Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, Portuguese, Russian, German, French, and Italian, with dates and numbers to match.

privacy.title: No account needed
privacy.body: No sign-in, and we don’t collect which apps you have installed. Malware scans run on your Mac, and your Brewfile list stays in your browser.

cta.title: Start with your next app.
cta.body: OpenNavo is free and open source, with malware scanning, cleanup and monitoring included. It runs on macOS 13 or later. You can also browse on the web and copy the brew command to install.
